methods.name: Remove the seasons (monthly anomalies)
methods.description: Subtract the average of each calendar month so summer/winter is not mistaken for a trend.

methods.name: Theil-Sen slope with 95% confidence interval
methods.description: A robust slope - the median of the slopes between all pairs of months.

methods.name: Mann-Kendall test with Hamed-Rao correction
methods.description: Is the trend real or luck? Corrected because each month resembles the previous one.

methods.name: Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate
methods.description: Testing hundreds of cells makes some look significant by chance; FDR corrects for it.

methods.name: Regional average weighted by cos(latitude)
methods.description: One series for the whole area, then the same slope and test.

methods.name: Years needed to detect the trend (Weatherhead 1998)
methods.description: For non-significant trends, how many years of data would be needed to be sure.

methods.name: Rank variables by significant area
methods.description: Which variable changes over the largest share of the area.

methods.name: Opposite-trend map and sub-region contrasts
methods.description: Find places moving in opposite directions that a regional average would hide.

methods.name: Trend-signature clusters (k-means, silhouette)
methods.description: Group cells that changed in a similar way. Clusters suggest, statistics decide.

answer:
## Short answer

Yes, the region is getting warmer, and its top layer of soil is drying out. Between 2001-01 and 2024-12, air temperature increased and soil moisture decreased across most of the area. Rainfall decreased slightly, but that change is not yet statistically certain.

## What the data shows

An anomaly is a difference from normal seasonal conditions. A trend is the general direction of change over time. The p-value measures the probability that a pattern happened purely by random chance. When a result is statistically significant, it means the pattern is very unlikely to be an accident.

- Air temperature at 2 m had a slope of 0.488 degC per decade for the period 2001-01 to 2024-12 [observed]. Its p-value is < 0.001, so this trend is significant [observed]. A significant increase occurred across 81.8 percent of the area, and 0 percent had a significant decrease [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) measures water in the upper ground layer. It had a slope of -0.585 kg m-2 per decade for the period 2001-01 to 2024-12 [observed]. Its p-value is < 0.001, so this drying trend is significant [observed]. About 58.3 percent of the area showed a significant decrease, while 8.9 percent showed a significant increase [observed].
- Precipitation had a slope of -1.18 mm/month per decade for the period 2001-01 to 2024-12 [observed]. Its p-value is 0.12, so this trend is not significant [observed]. Only 6.4 percent of the area had a significant decrease, and 2.6 percent had a significant increase [observed].
- Vegetation greenness (NDVI) tracks plant health and cover. It had a slope of 0.00617 NDVI units per decade for the period 2001-01 to 2024-12 [observed]. Its p-value is < 0.001, so this greening trend is significant [observed]. A significant increase covered 42.5 percent of the area, and 7.6 percent had a significant decrease [observed].

## Places moving in opposite directions

Not all subregions experienced soil drying in the same way [observed].

- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) increased in Nile Delta and Lower Egypt with a slope of 0.0773 kg m-2 per decade [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) decreased in Iberian Peninsula with a slope of -0.755 kg m-2 per decade [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) decreased in Italy and the Balkans with a slope of -0.732 kg m-2 per decade [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) decreased in Levant with a slope of -0.174 kg m-2 per decade [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) decreased in Maghreb with a slope of -1.07 kg m-2 per decade [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) decreased in Sahara margin with a slope of -0.301 kg m-2 per decade [observed].
- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) decreased in Tunisia with a slope of -0.936 kg m-2 per decade [observed].

## What scientists have written

In the paper "Evidence of increasing drought severity caused by temperature rise in southern Europe" (2014), researchers noted that rising temperatures increase evaporative demand, citing "greater atmospheric evaporative demand resulting from temperature rise" [literature].

## Possible explanations

These ideas are hypotheses, meaning they are untested proposals and are not proven. Correlation does not equal causation.

- Soil moisture (0-10 cm) increases in Nile Delta and Lower Egypt but decreases in Iberian Peninsula, Italy and the Balkans, Levant, Maghreb, Sahara margin, Tunisia: different processes may dominate in each place, and a single regional average hides this [hypothesis].
- The places in the warming and drying groups could be compound heat-and-drought hot spots worth watching; clustering only shows that these places changed in a similar way [hypothesis].

## Limits of this investigation

- The rainfall trend has a p-value of 0.12 and is not statistically significant. Detecting a clear trend for precipitation would require 39.8 years of data.
- The soil moisture data only reflects the shallow surface layer from 0-10 cm. It does not measure deep groundwater.
- We cannot declare that warming caused the drying based solely on these statistics.
